analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 20% minimum tax on household wealth above $100 million, counting gains before assets are sold.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced in July 2022, it died there when the Congress ended in January 2023, despite 55 Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require anyone with a net worth over $100 million to pay a minimum tax of 20% on their income plus the increase in the value of their unsold assets each year. Under current law, gains on assets a wealthy person never sells are not taxed at all, so someone can grow rich on paper and owe little or no federal income tax. The bill also stops common workarounds, such as giving assets away or passing them to heirs tax-free, and caps the tax so no one owes more than 40% of their wealth above the $100 million line.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the direct beneficiaries would be everyone who does not have nine-figure wealth: the tax reaches only households worth over $100 million, and its revenue would have reduced deficits or funded public priorities as Congress chose. Wealthy taxpayers would also get credit for the minimum tax when they eventually sell assets, so gains would not be taxed twice.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a minimum tax of 20% on the sum of a taxpayer's income and net unrealized gains for each year that their net worth exceeds $100 million.
Caps the tax at 40% of the amount by which the taxpayer's net worth exceeds $100 million, so no one owes more than that share of their wealth above the threshold.
Lets wealthy taxpayers pay in installments (nine in the first year, five thereafter) and gives credit against later tax when gains are actually realized, so the same gain is not taxed twice.
Closes avoidance routes by taxing gifts, charitable bequests, and transfers at death by covered taxpayers, and by treating certain trusts as subject to the tax.
States the sense of Congress that state-level taxes on extreme wealth are in the public interest, clearing the way for states to adopt their own.

analysis.who_pays: The roughly 0.01% of households whose net worth exceeds $100 million, who would owe tax each year on the appreciation of assets they have not sold. No household below that threshold pays anything under the bill.

drawbacks.text: Valuing assets that are not traded on public markets (private companies, art, land) is hard and contested. The bill handles this with default formulas, Treasury regulations, and a special valuation regime that taxpayers can challenge only on a showing of clear and convincing error, which is workable but adds real administrative complexity and dispute risk.

Owners of fast-growing private businesses could owe tax on paper gains before any money reaches them. The bill softens this with installment plans, a lower threshold for 'illiquid' taxpayers, and a deferred tax reserve for non-tradable assets, but it remains the strongest practical objection to taxing unrealized gains.

Critics argue that taxing an asset's increase in value before it is sold stretches the constitutional definition of taxable 'income.' That argument has never been resolved and would likely have drawn lawsuits had the bill advanced.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aims at a real gap: under current law, gains on assets never sold are never taxed, which is how many of the wealthiest households avoid income tax entirely. It is aimed narrowly and includes serious guardrails (installments, credits against later sales, deferred treatment of illiquid assets), which keeps the hardship objection smaller than in cruder versions of a wealth tax. The main honest cost is administrative: valuing private assets annually would be complicated and disputed. On balance the costs fall on a tiny group with ample means to manage them, and the design addresses the hardest objections.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote; it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the Billionaire Minimum Income Tax Act on July 28, 2022, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
The bill attracted 55 cosponsors, all Democrats, including senior members such as Rosa DeLauro and Jerrold Nadler.
No further action of any kind followed the referral: no hearing, no markup, no vote, and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The bill closely tracked the 'billionaire minimum income tax' proposal in the Biden administration's budget, which would have applied a similar 20% tax on households worth over $100 million.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households with more than $100 million in net worth are better off: they continue to owe no federal tax on gains from assets they never sell, and the mechanics of borrowing against appreciated assets remain untouched. The tax-writing committee's inaction preserved that status quo without a single member having to vote on it.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Billionaire Minimum Income Tax Act and recruited 55 cosponsors for it.

for.name: 55 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none of them held a committee chair position that could advance it.

for.name: President Joe Biden
for.what_they_did: Proposed an essentially identical billionaire minimum income tax in his budget, setting the policy template for the bill.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; the committee took no action after the referral, and the bill died there.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat and no Republican supported the bill, but it never reached a vote, so there was no roll call to measure the split.

industries.industry: Households with net worth above $100 million
industries.note: The tax would reach their unsold asset gains each year, which currently go untaxed, and would tax gifts and bequests they now use to move wealth without recognizing gain. Their saving comes directly at the cost of the revenue the rest of the tax base would otherwise provide.

industries.industry: Private equity, venture capital, and founders of private companies
industries.note: Stakes in private companies are the classic untaxed unrealized gain; the bill's rules for non-readily tradable assets would tax that appreciation on a deferred or installment basis rather than letting it ride until an eventual sale.
Annual valuations, reporting, and reserve-account rules would generate substantial new compliance work for advisors to the very wealthy, even as their clients' tax bills rise.
